Effects of Bradyrhizobium, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Pseudomonas putida on Cowpea 
(Vigna unguiculata) Plant Yield in Martian Regolith Soil. 
Samrawit Ameha, Haleigh Dunaski, Amanda Hang, Katelynn Peterson. 
 
Background: 
Human exploration of Mars presents substantial logistical and physiological challenges, 
especially because missions require extended time away from Earth. A full round-trip may last 
nearly three years, during which astronauts face muscle loss, radiation exposure, and overall 
physiological decline. Sustainable food production systems, therefore, become essential, as they 
provide nutrition, psychological comfort, and reduce reliance on resupply missions (Buckey 
1999). One major obstacle in doing so is that Martian regolith lacks organic material and 
contains very low levels of plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. These nutrients 
are fundamental for biomass accumulation, metabolism, and reproduction, which means that 
successful crop growth will require strategies that compensate for these nutrient deficits. 
Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) has emerged as a strong candidate for extraterrestrial agriculture 
due to its rapid growth, drought tolerance, and natural symbiotic relationship with 
Bradyrhizobium, a nitrogen-fixing bacterium (Nyoki 2014). This relationship enables cowpeas to 
convert atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) into ammonia (NH₃), providing the plant with essential 
nitrogen without the need for fertilizer input. One of the most visible outcomes of successful 
inoculation in legumes is the development of root nodules, which house nitrogen-fixing bacteria. 
These nodules serve as biological fertilizer units, ensuring that plants can access usable nitrogen 
even when growing in nutrient-poor systems such as regolith. Nitrogen fixation, however, is 
energetically expensive and heavily depends on phosphorus, as it supports ATP production 
necessary for nitrogenase activity. Under low phosphorus conditions, legumes tend to produce 
fewer nodules, smaller nodules, and exhibit less efficient nitrogen fixation (Divito et al. 2013). 
Potassium further influences legume development by regulating photosynthesis, carbohydrate 
allocation, water balance, and enzyme activity. Duke and Collins (1985) showed that increasing 
potassium availability improved both nitrogen assimilation and reproductive outcomes by 
supporting enzyme function in legume nodules. 
These nutrient constraints have led researchers to explore microbial solutions that mobilize 
nutrients directly in the root zone. Pseudomonas fluorescens is widely studied for its ability to 
solubilize phosphorus through the secretion of organic acids and phosphatase, which improves 
phosphorus uptake and enhances the nitrogen-fixation process (Sharma et al. 2013). Additional 
support for combining microbes comes from Jabborova et al. (2018), who found that soybean 
plants co-inoculated with Bradyrhizobium japonicum and Pseudomonas putida developed more 
nodules, stronger root systems, and greater biomass than plants inoculated with Bradyrhizobium 
alone. These improvements were observed at both low and high phosphorus levels, indicating

that P. putida enhances nutrient acquisition across a wide range of environments. This evidence 
reinforces the idea that nutrient-mobilizing bacteria can enhance the performance of 
nitrogen-fixing microbes, rather than acting independently. 
Our experiment applies these findings by testing whether inoculating cowpea with 
Bradyrhizobium, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Pseudomonas putida improves nodulation and 
reproductive growth in a 50% Martian regolith mixture. The broader scientific question is 
whether microbial consortia can operate as self-sustaining fertilizers in environments lacking 
nutrient inputs. If cowpea produces more nodules, greater biomass, and higher fruit output under 
inoculated treatments, this would suggest that microbe-supported agriculture could contribute to 
long-term food systems beyond Earth. These findings also extend to Earth-based challenges, 
where similar microbial interactions could improve food production in nutrient-poor or degraded 
soils. 
Hypothesis 
If cowpea plants grown in a 50% Martian regolith mixture are inoculated with 
phosphorus-solubilizing (Pseudomonas fluorescens) and potassium-associated (Pseudomonas 
putida) microbes in addition to Bradyrhizobium, then plants receiving all three microbes will 
produce a greater number of fruits and develop larger and more abundant nodules than plants 
receiving only Bradyrhizobium. This outcome is expected because the combined microbial 
activity is expected to increase the bioavailability of essential nutrients, particularly phosphorus 
and potassium, which enhances nitrogen-fixation efficiency and supports healthy reproductive 
growth (Divito et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2013; Duke and Collins, 1985). 
Rationale 
Plants receiving the combination of nitrogen-fixing and nutrient-mobilizing microbes are 
expected to outperform the other treatments. Nitrogen fixation by Bradyrhizobium enhances 
growth and leaf development, while sufficient phosphorus availability improves nitrogenase 
function and overall nodule formation (Divito et al., 2013). Pseudomonas fluorescens enhances 
phosphorus bioavailability, thereby improving the efficiency of ATP-dependent nitrogen fixation 
and promoting biomass accumulation (Sharma et al., 2013). Pseudomonas putida has been 
linked to maintaining favorable root-microbe interactions, which enhance physiological 
resilience and nutrient uptake (Jabborova et al., 2018). Together, these bacteria create a 
nutrient-supportive environment that is predicted to yield stronger plant growth, more nodules, 
and greater fruiting success than cowpea growing with Bradyrhizobium alone.

Methods 
A total of twelve pots were used, three for each treatment type. Treatments included a control 
inoculated only with Bradyrhizobium, NP inoculated with Bradyrhizobium and Pseudomonas 
fluorescens, NK inoculated with Bradyrhizobium and Pseudomonas putida, and NPK inoculated 
with all three bacteria. All treatments received a 50% mixture of regolith and 50% soil in the top 
chamber, while the bottom chamber with a wick received 200 milliliters of distilled water for the 
first week, followed by 100 milliliters of water each week. Cowpea seeds were soaked in 
distilled water overnight in a controlled growth chamber before being placed in pots. Each pot 
received three seeds without inoculation. Three weeks later, the plants were inoculated with 
Bradyrhizobium (a Nitrogen fixer), Pseudomonas fluorescens (a Phosphorus solubilizer), and 
Pseudomonas putida (a Potassium solubilizer). Observations were recorded weekly in a lab 
notebook, including nutrient deficiencies, stem length, overall plant health, and growth. 
Additionally, weekly photographs were taken. A dilution series was completed after the initial 
inoculation to measure how many CFUs would be present in the soil 
 
 
Results 
Across the 7-week growth period, all four treatment groups showed a steady increase in stem 
length. The NK treatment reached the highest average stem length by week 7, followed by NPK 
and NP treatments, while the control remained slightly lower (Figure 1). Leaf number also 
increased over time across all treatment groups, and by week 7, the NP and NPK treatments had 
the highest average number of leaves, with the NK treatment being slightly lower, and the 
control showing the fewest number of leaves (Figure 2). At the end of the growth period, the 
plants were harvested to measure root length and biomass. The treatment group with the highest 
average root length was the control group, while NP, NK, and NPK treatments displayed similar 
values (Figure 3). Measurements of biomass followed a similar pattern, with the control group 
having the highest average biomass, followed by NP, NK, and NPK showed the lowest averages 
(Figure 4). Error bars overlapped across most treatment groups and their measurements. There 
were obvious nutrient deficiencies, such as chlorosis, noted by light green discoloration and 
white or yellow spots on the leaves. Molybdenum deficiency is another condition often indicated 
by scorched leaves. When the plants were harvested, and root measurements were being taken, 
the roots were investigated for nodule growth. There were no visible nodules on any of the roots 
throughout all treatments. However, a dilution series of the soil was conducted to test whether 
bacteria were present in the soil. The dilution series demonstrated bacterial growth on the plates, 
indicating that it also occurred in the soil of each treatment.

Figure 1. Average stem length for 4 treatment groups over a 7-week period. Stem lengths 
were measured on each plant per treatment throughout the growth period. The plants were 
replanted in week one, so there is no data available. However, the plants germinated and were 
measured starting in week 2. Throughout the growth period, the NK treatment appears to have 
the largest average stem length. Error bars represent ±1 standard error.

Figure 2. Average number of leaves per plant in 4 treatment groups over a 7-week period. 
The average number of leaves was counted on each plant per treatment throughout the growth 
period. There is no data for week one because the plants were replanted, and the data was 
collected for weeks 2-7. NP had the most leaves by the end of the growth period, but in weeks 
1-5, NK had the most leaves. Error bars represent ±1 standard error.

Figure 3. Average root length across four treatment groups. There were four treatments: 
control, nitrogen-phosphorus, nitrogen-potassium, and nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium. The 
plants were grown in a planting chamber for 7 weeks, and then, at the end of the growth period, 
all plant roots were cleaned and measured. The control group had the largest root length; 
however, none of the data appears to be statistically significant, as indicated by the overlapping 
error bars. Error bars represent ±1 standard error.

Figure 4. Average Biomass across four treatment groups. There were four treatment groups: 
control, containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria; nitrogen-phosphorus, containing nitrogen-fixing 
bacteria and phosphorus-solubilizing bacteria; nitrogen-potassium, containing nitrogen-fixing 
bacteria and potassium-solubilizing bacteria; and nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium, containing all 
three bacteria. The control group had the highest biomass, and the data between the control 
group and the NP group are statistically significant. The remaining data is not statistically 
significant. Error bars represent ±1 standard error.

Figure 5. Week 2 Growth Progress. Plant growth is shown two weeks after planting. Panels 
show different treatment conditions: (A) NK, (B) NPK, (C) NP, (D) control. All treatments show 
relatively healthy plants with ongoing vegetative growth.

Figure 6. Week 7 Growth Progress. Plant growth is shown at the final week of treatment. 
Panels show: (A) NK, (B) NPK, (C) NP, (D) control. Notable symptoms of nutrient deficiency 
are evident across all conditions, suggesting widespread stress and nutrient depletion in the soil 
medium.

Discussion 
 
Final results after the 7-week growth period showed that our hypothesis was not supported. We 
hypothesized that the NPK group would have the largest and most abundant root nodules, as well 
as a greater number of fruits. None of the treatment groups developed any root nodules during 
the growth period. There was also no fruit production during the growth period. This is not 
surprising considering that cowpeas, Vigna unguiculata, take at least 60 days to produce pods 
before the formation of mature seeds, and the growth period was less than 60 days (Growing 
staple vegetables from around the world in Minnesota, 2021). There is a possibility that the root 
nodules were unable to form because the inoculation with Bradyrhizobium did not occur until 
three weeks after the seeds had been planted, allowing them time to grow without the presence of 
the bacteria. Although a dilution series was conducted and the presence of bacteria in each of the 
treatment groups was confirmed, further testing would be needed to determine the specific type 
of bacteria present in the substrates. The ideal way to identify each of the different species of 
bacteria would be to sequence each of the colonies on the dilution series plates to confirm their 
identification. The presence of bacteria after the growth period is suggestive that microbes have 
the ability to survive in a substrate that contains at least 50% Mars regolith. 
 
The overall growth of the plants across each treatment group showed no significant differences 
in average stem length, number of leaves, root length, or biomass. The lack of significant 
differences between the treatment groups is possibly due to the fact that inoculation of the 
microbes Pseudomonas fluorescens, Pseudomonas putida, and Bradyrhizobium occurred later in 
the growth period. This could also be the reason behind the apparent nutrient deficiencies 
observed in each of the treatment groups. Chlorosis was observed on many leaves, characterized 
by a yellowish discoloration accompanied by white and yellow spots. Interveinal chlorosis was 
shown by the light green along the veins only. A molybdenum deficiency was also noticed in the 
plants, which appeared as scorched leaves. Molybdenum is important for enzymatic activity and 
nitrogen fixation in legume plants (McCauley et al. 2009). The plant's inability to uptake and 
obtain necessary nutrients from the substrate to combat nutrient deficiencies could be due to the 
lack of solubilizing microbes in the substrate or a substrate pH outside the range for optimal 
nutrient uptake. 
 
For future direction, monitoring the pH of the substrate would be beneficial to determine which 
nutrients can be taken up by the plants. If the pH appears to be out of range for specific nutrients, 
such as Nitrogen, Phosphorus, or Potassium uptake, actions can be taken to adjust the pH in the 
substrate to facilitate proper nutrient uptake. Another suggestion for future research would be to 
plant either one or two seeds per pot to lower the competition for nutrients between plants. 
Fighting for nutrients can be an additional stressor on the plants during experimental growth 
periods. Furthermore, inoculating the different microbes immediately after seed germination, 
rather than waiting for plant growth, could allow more time for the microbes to fix nitrogen for

the plants and solubilize nutrients such as phosphorus and potassium in the substrate during the 
critical growth and survival stages. 
 
 
 
 
 
Annotated Bibliography: 
 
1.​ Buckey JC. 1999. Preparing for Mars: the physiologic and medical challenges. PubMed. 
4(9):353–6. 
Buckey discusses the physiological risks associated with long-term space travel, including 
radiation exposure, bone loss, muscle deterioration, and cardiovascular strain. The article 
highlights how limited resupply missions force astronauts to rely on sustainable life-support 
systems. This source directly supports the justification for developing self-sustaining food 
systems in space, reinforcing the need for agricultural solutions like microbial-assisted plant 
growth. 
2.​ Divito GA, Sadras VO. 2014. How do phosphorus, potassium and sulphur affect plant 
growth and biological nitrogen fixation in crop and pasture legumes? A 
meta-analysis. Field Crops Research. 156:161–171. 
doi:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fcr.2013.11.004. [accessed 2020 May 19]. 
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378429013003833. 
This meta-analysis examines nutrient limitations and their effects on legume growth and nitrogen 
fixation. The research shows that phosphorus shortages reduce nodule size and number, while 
potassium influences root metabolism, carbohydrate transport, and nitrogen assimilation. This 
article supports the rationale for adding nutrient-mobilizing microbes in your study, since 
Martian regolith lacks P and K, and your hypothesis predicts these microbes will enhance nodule 
formation.

3.​ Duke SH, Collins M. 2015 Nov 2. Role of Potassium in Legume Dinitrogen Fixation. 
ASSA, CSSA and SSSA.:443–465. 
doi:https://doi.org/10.2134/1985.potassium.c19. 
This book section examines the role of potassium in nitrogen assimilation and nodule enzyme 
activity, with a focus on glutamine synthetase. Findings show that potassium supplementation 
increases both nitrogen fixation and crop yield in legumes. This source directly informs 
expectations that treatments involving Pseudomonas putida should lead to stronger growth, 
nodulation, and fruit outcomes by improving nutrient cycling pathways. 
4.​ Ehlers JD, Hall AE. 1997. Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata L. Walp.). Field Crops Research. 
[accesed 2025 September 26];53(1-3):187-204. 
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378429097000312?casa_token=OqT
bXVdxeN0AAAAA:lBvTACbMsAODUB6Q_7q1NVFqDRRLyj0VQekCmocACbPC5D 
R7wxrQTET-3iIVGE_JoZAR4iid. doi: https://doi.org/10.1016/S0378-4290(97)00031-2. 
Ehlers and Hall discussed how Vigna unguiculata (Cowpea) is an adapted and stress-tolerant 
legume species. Scientists have developed Cowpea that shows resistance to important diseases 
and pests. This plant is capable of growing in diverse cropping systems and is drought-tolerant. 
The authors are particularly interested in Vigna unguiculata due to its potential as a drought- and 
heat-tolerant plant, as well as its resistance to insects and pests. 
5.​ Fackrell LE, Humphrey S, Loureiro R, Palmer AG, Long-Fox J. 2024. Overview and 
recommendations for research on plants and microbes in regolith-based agriculture. Npj 
Sustainable Agriculture. [accessed 2025 September 26]; 2(1). 
https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-024-00013-5. 
Doi:https://doi.org/10.1038/s44264-024-00013-5. 
Fackrell and colleagues discussed the idea that humans want to establish and maintain a presence 
on the moon and possibly other planets. To successfully grow plants on the moon or any other 
planet, a robust and sustainable crop production system must be developed. The system analyzed

in this paper was regolith-based agriculture (RBA). RBA is not very well studied, so the authors 
propose a need for standardized practices when working with RBA. 
6.​ Growing staple vegetables from around the world in Minnesota. 2021. Umnedu. 
[accessed 2025 Dec]. 
https://extension.umn.edu/vegetables/growing-staple-vegetables-around-world-minnesota
#cowpea-%28vigna-unguiculata%29-3342612. 
This webpage is from the University of Minnesota that features growing guides for different 
vegetables from around the world. It states the expected time period for how long it takes 
cowpeas to produce their pods and when the seeds mature. 
7.​ Jabborova D, Enakiev Y, Davranov K, Sh. A. B. 2018. Effect of co-inoculation with 
bradyrhizobium japonicum and pseudomonas putida on root morph-architecture traits, 
nodulation and growth of soybean in response to phosphorus supply under hydroponic 
conditions. ResearchGate. [accessed 2025 Dec 5]. 
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/332094434_Effect_of_co-inoculation_with_bra
dyrhizobium_japonicum_and_pseudomonas_putida_on_root_morph-architecture_traits_n
odulation_and_growth_of_soybean_in_response_to_phosphorus_supply_under_hydropo
nic_condi. 
Jabborova and colleagues investigated how co-inoculation of soybean roots with Bradyrhizobium 
japonicum and Pseudomonas putida affected root development, nodulation, and growth under 
different phosphorus levels. The study showed that plants receiving both microbes developed 
larger nodules, a greater number of nodules, and stronger root structure compared to plants 
inoculated with only Bradyrhizobium. Improvements occurred in both low- and high-phosphorus 
nutrient conditions, suggesting that P. putida supports nutrient uptake and enhances nitrogen 
fixation efficiency. This research is relevant to our experiment because it demonstrates that 
combining nitrogen-fixing bacteria with nutrient-mobilizing bacteria strengthens nodulation 
performance and overall plant growth. Therefore, similar improvements are expected in cowpea 
when Bradyrhizobium, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Pseudomonas putida are present together.

8.​ Mccauley Ann, et al. Nutrient Management a Self-Study Course from the MSU Extension 
Service Continuing Education Series Plant Nutrient Functions and Deficiency and 
Toxicity Symptoms. 2009. 
Mccauley and colleagues mapped out a list of common nutrient deficiencies found in plants. 
They created an easy-to-read flow chart for readers to think about what nutrient deficiencies their 
plants may be experiencing. There is also a wealth of information about the causes of nutrient 
deficiencies. Information that was specifically important to this research pertained to chlorosis, 
interveinal chlorosis, magnesium deficiencies, and molybdenum deficiency. leaves 
9.​ Mira P, Yeh P, Hall BG. 2022. Estimating Microbial Population Data from Optical 
Density. Omri A, editor. PLOS ONE. 17(10):e0276040. 
doi:https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0276040. 
This paper reviews the importance of calibrating the spectrophotometer that is used to measure 
bacterial population densities. It is relevant to the research because it shows the number of 
cells/mL at OD 1 for P. putida. 
10.​Nikfarjam SG, Aminpanah H. 2015. Effects of Phosphorus Fertilization and 
Pseudomonas fluorescens Strain on the Growth and Yield of Faba Bean (Vicia faba L.). 
[accessed 2025 September 26];3:15-21. 
https://scielo.conicyt.cl/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0718-34292015000400003. 
Nikfarjam and Aminpanah conducted an experiment to determine the effect of phosphorus 
solubilization and Pseudomonas fluorescens on the growth of a faba bean. There was a 
significant interaction effect of phosphorus and P. fluorescens on plant height, pod number per 
plant, pod yield, and grain yield. 
11.​Nyoki D, Ndakidemi PA. 2014. Effects of Phosphorus and Bradyrhizobium japonicum on 
Growth and Chlorophyll Content of Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata (L) Walp). American

Journal of Experimental Agriculture. 4(10):1120–1136. 
doi:https://doi.org/10.9734/ajea/2014/6736. 
Nyoki and Ndakidemi demonstrate that supplying phosphorus and inoculating with 
Bradyrhizobium significantly improves cowpea leaf chlorophyll content, biomass, and root 
nodulation. Their findings reinforce that nitrogen fixation requires both proper rhizobial 
colonization and sufficient phosphorus availability. This article helps justify your expected 
treatment differences and the prediction that adding phosphorus-solubilizing bacteria leads to 
larger nodules and greater plant yield. 
12.​Sharma SB, Sayyed RZ, Trivedi MH, Gobi TA. 2013. Phosphate solubilizing microbes: 
sustainable approach for managing phosphorus deficiency in agricultural soils. 
SpringerPlus. 2(1). doi:https://doi.org/10.1186/2193-1801-2-587. 
This paper reviews how PSB increases phosphorus availability by producing organic acids, 
enzymes, and by releasing phosphate from insoluble compounds. PSB treatment is associated 
with enhanced root development, improved nitrogen fixation, and increased grain yield. This 
directly supports the inclusion of Pseudomonas fluorescens in your experiment and helps explain 
the mechanism connecting phosphorus availability to reproductive success. 
13.​Zhang T, Hu F, Ma L. 2019. Phosphate-solubilizing bacteria from safflower rhizosphere 
and their effect on seedling growth. Open Life Sciences. 14(1):246–254. 
doi:https://doi.org/10.1515/biol-2019-0028. 
This paper reviews phosphate-solubilizing bacteria that can enhance plant growth. The methods 
and results of this study gave the suggested amount of CFUs that should be added to the plants 
for optimal growth.
